chapters.name: Chapter 1: Your phone as a helper

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Reminders and alarms by voice
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set a reminder for an appointment by speaking to your phone.
This lesson builds toward: Using your phone's voice assistant, you will set a reminder for an appointment and a second reminder for when to leave, by voice, with a general title and no private details.
Missing an appointment can cost you a job interview, a housing spot or a check-in. Your phone can remember for you.
Most phones have a voice assistant: Siri on iPhone, and Google Assistant or Gemini on Android. Wake it by saying "Hey Siri" or "Hey Google", or by pressing and holding the side or home button. Then say: "Remind me about my interview at Fresh Foods on Tuesday at 9 am." "Set an alarm for 6:30 am tomorrow."
Set two reminders for anything important: one the day before, and one when it is time to leave. Keep reminder titles general; you do not need to put private details in them.
Step by step:
- Wake the voice assistant.
- Say what, the day and the time.
- Add a second reminder for when to leave.
- Check the screen to make sure it is set.
Words to know:
- Voice assistant: a helper built into your phone that does simple tasks when you speak.
- Reminder: a message your phone shows you at a time you choose.
Try it now: Set a reminder by voice for a real appointment, or a practice one, and a second reminder for when you need to leave.
You can now set appointment reminders and alarms by voice.

check.q: What is a good title for a reminder about a job interview?
options: Your full name and date of birth
check.why: Reminder titles should be general, without private details.

check.q: Your interview is tomorrow at 9 am and the bus takes 40 minutes. What would you do?
options: Hope you remember in the morning
Set a reminder for tonight and one for when to leave
check.why: Two reminders, the day before and when to leave, help you arrive on time.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Getting around with maps and transit
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Get bus, train or walking directions and know when to leave.
This lesson builds toward: Given the address of a real place, you will get bus, train or walking directions in a maps app and find when to leave, with an arrival time set to 10 to 15 minutes early.
Maps apps such as Google Maps and Apple Maps show how to get anywhere by bus, train, walking or car, and how long it will take.
Open the maps app, type the address in the search box, and tap Directions. Choose the bus or train symbol for transit, or the walking person. You will see which bus to take, where to catch it, and when it comes. You can also set the time you need to arrive, and the app shows when to leave.
Plan to arrive 10 to 15 minutes early. Buses can run late. Save addresses you visit often, such as your home or work, so they are one tap away. Some transit agencies also have their own apps with live bus times.
Step by step:
- Open your maps app.
- Type the address and tap Directions.
- Choose transit (bus or train) or walking.
- Set your arrival time to see when to leave.
- Plan to arrive 10 to 15 minutes early.
Words to know:
- Transit: public transportation such as buses and trains.
- Arrival time: the time you need to be there.
Try it now: Get transit or walking directions to a real place you need to go, such as an American Job Center, the DMV or a library. Set the arrival time and note when you must leave.
You can now get transit and walking directions and work out when to leave.

check.q: What does setting your arrival time in a maps app show you?
check.why: With an arrival time set, the app works out when you need to leave.

check.q: You need to reach the DMV by bus for a 10 am visit. What would you do?
options: Get transit directions and set arrival for about 9:45
Ask a stranger at the stop
check.why: Transit directions with an early arrival time help you get there 10 to 15 minutes early.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reading and translating with your camera
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use your phone's camera to read, copy or translate printed text.
This lesson builds toward: Given a printed flyer, sign or job posting, you will use your phone's camera to read, copy or translate its text, copying a phone number or address into a note or contact without retyping it.
Your phone's camera can read printed words. With Google Lens (in the Google app and on many Android phones) or the iPhone camera's text feature, you can point at a flyer, a sign or a form and copy the text, look it up, or translate it.
Open the camera or Google Lens and point at the words. Tap the text button or the highlighted text, then choose Copy, Listen, Translate or Search. This is helpful for copying a phone number from a flyer or reading instructions in another language.
Do not scan documents with private numbers into AI tools, such as your Social Security card or court papers. Use these tools for public things like flyers, signs and job postings.
Step by step:
- Open the camera or Google Lens.
- Point at the printed words.
- Tap the text button or the highlighted words.
- Choose Copy, Listen, Translate or Search.
- Do not scan private documents.
Words to know:
- Google Lens: a free Google tool that uses your camera to read, translate and search what it sees.
- Translate: change words from one language into another.
Try it now: Point your camera or Google Lens at a flyer, sign or job posting. Copy a phone number or address from it into a note or your contacts.
You can now use your camera to copy, hear or translate printed text.

check.q: What can your phone's camera text tool do with a printed job flyer?
options: Apply for the job for you
Read, copy or translate the text
check.why: The camera text tool can read, copy and translate printed words.

check.q: You want to scan a paper with your Social Security number into an AI tool. What would you do?
options: Scan it so the AI can explain it
Do not scan it; keep private numbers out of AI tools
check.why: Private numbers like your Social Security number should never go into AI tools.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding local help
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find local services for housing, food, jobs or transportation.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant and 211, you will find a local service for housing, food, jobs or transportation, with one program written down and its details confirmed through 211 or an official site.
There is help available, but finding it can be hard. 211 is a service across the United States that connects you with local help for housing, food, transportation, health care and more. Call 211, or search for your local 211 at 211.org. Calls are confidential and you can stay anonymous.
An AI assistant can help you prepare: "I just came home and live in Columbus, Ohio. What kinds of local services might help with housing, food, and job training? What questions should I ask when I call 211?"
AI may list programs that closed or give wrong phone numbers. Always confirm with 211, the program's official website, or your reentry case manager before you go.
Step by step:
- Ask AI what kinds of help to look for and what to ask.
- Call 211 or search 211.org.
- Write down the programs, numbers and hours.
- Confirm on the official website or by phone before you go.
Words to know:
- 211: a phone number and website that connect you with local help.
- Case manager: a person who helps you plan and find services.
Official sources:
- 211: About us
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant what kinds of local services could help you right now and what to ask when you call. Then look up your local 211 at 211.org and write down one program to contact.
You can now find local help and confirm it before you go.

options: Only job openings at big companies
Local help for housing, food and more
check.why: 211 connects people to local services like housing and food help.

check.q: An AI assistant gives you the phone number of a food bank. What would you do?
options: Confirm the number with 211 or the official site
Share it with friends without checking
Ask AI if it is sure
check.why: AI can be wrong, so you confirm details with 211 or an official source.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Writing everyday messages with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to write a short, polite message for a real situation.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real everyday situation, you will write a short, polite message with AI help, that is honest, has no private details and sounds like you.
Many everyday situations need a message: telling an employer you will be late, asking a landlord about an apartment, thanking someone for an interview, or reaching out to family.
Tell the AI who it is for, what you need to say, and how it should sound: "Write a short, polite text to a hiring manager. My bus is running 10 minutes late for my 9 am interview. I am sorry and still very interested."
Read it out loud and change anything that does not sound like you. Keep it short and honest. You do not need to explain your past in everyday messages.
Step by step:
- Say who it is for.
- Say what you need to say.
- Say how it should sound: polite, short, friendly.
- Read it aloud and make it sound like you.
Words to know:
- Polite: respectful and courteous.
- Draft: a first version you can change.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to write a short, polite text telling an interviewer your bus is running late. Change one thing so it sounds like you.
You can now write clear, polite everyday messages with AI help.

check.q: What makes an everyday message good?
options: Long and full of details about your past
check.why: A short, polite, honest message is easy to read and respectful.

check.q: AI wrote a late text that uses words you would never say. What would you do?
options: Ask AI to make it longer
Delete it and not send anything
Change the words so it sounds like you, then send it
check.why: You read AI drafts and change them so they sound like you.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Checklists for appointments and documents
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask AI for a checklist of what to bring, then confirm it with the office.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real appointment, you will make a checklist of what to bring with AI help and confirm it with the office, listing document names only, checked on the official site or by phone.
Showing up without the right papers can mean a second trip. Ask AI for a checklist: "I am going to my state's DMV to get a state ID. What documents do people usually need to bring? Make a short checklist."
Then confirm with the office itself. Rules differ by state and change over time, so the official website (often ending in .gov) or a phone call is the final word. Your reentry program or case manager may also help you get documents such as a birth certificate.
Keep the checklist in your phone's notes or on paper. Never type your actual ID numbers, case numbers or Social Security number into AI; the checklist only needs the names of documents.
Step by step:
- Ask AI what is usually needed.
- Ask for a short checklist.
- Confirm on the office's official website or by phone.
- Gather the papers and check them off.
- Never type your real numbers into AI.
Words to know:
- Checklist: a list of items you tick off one by one.
- State ID: an official photo ID card from your state, for people who do not drive.
Try it now: Final task: pick a real appointment. Get transit or walking directions, set a reminder for when to leave, ask AI for a checklist of what to bring (then confirm it on the official site), and have AI help you write a short text to send if you are running late.
You can now use everyday AI tools to plan, prepare for and get to an appointment on time.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Directions No directions, or no idea when to leave. Transit or walking directions with an arrival time set early, and the leave time written down. Also has a backup route or the address saved for one-tap use. Reminder to leave No reminder, or a reminder with private details in the title. A reminder set for when to leave, with a general title. Also set a reminder the day before. Checklist confirmed No checklist, or a checklist with private numbers, or not confirmed. A checklist of document names, confirmed on the official site or by phone. Can say where they confirmed it and what changed from AI's list. Running-late text No text, or a text that is long, rude or has private details. A short, polite, honest text ready to send. The learner changed some words so it sounds like them. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What should a document checklist list?
options: The names of the documents you need
Your ID and Social Security numbers
check.why: A checklist needs document names, not your private numbers.

check.q: AI's checklist for a state ID visit looks complete. What would you do next?
options: Confirm the list on the office's official site or by phone
Ask a friend what they brought years ago
check.why: The office has the final word on what to bring.
